note: Curated GENERAL-WELLNESS knowledge base for DailyMinder's on-device assistant. Plain-language, non-diagnostic. NOT medical advice; a qualified clinician should review before a production release. Bump 'version' to re-seed.

chunks.title: The four cycle phases
chunks.body: A typical menstrual cycle has four phases: menstrual (your period), follicular (after your period, when an egg matures), ovulation (the egg is released), and luteal (after ovulation until your next period). Phase lengths vary from person to person.

chunks.title: Typical cycle length
chunks.body: Cycle length is commonly around 21 to 35 days and is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. It's normal for it to vary by a few days between cycles.

chunks.title: Follicular phase
chunks.body: The follicular phase starts on the first day of your period and lasts until ovulation. Estrogen rises as an egg matures. Many people feel more energetic later in this phase.

chunks.title: Ovulation
chunks.body: Ovulation is when an ovary releases an egg, often roughly midway through the cycle. Calendar estimates of the day are approximate and can shift, especially with irregular cycles.

chunks.title: Luteal phase
chunks.body: The luteal phase runs from ovulation to your next period, usually about 12 to 14 days. Premenstrual symptoms are common in the days before your period.

chunks.title: Fertile window (estimate only)
chunks.body: The fertile window is roughly the five days before ovulation plus ovulation day. Calendar-based estimates are approximate and are NOT reliable for contraception; talk to a clinician about contraception options.

chunks.title: PMS symptoms
chunks.body: Premenstrual syndrome can include mood changes, bloating, tender breasts, cramps and fatigue in the week or two before your period. Regular sleep, movement and hydration may help some people.

chunks.title: Irregular cycles
chunks.body: Cycles that are very short, very long, or highly unpredictable are common at times, but persistent irregularity, very heavy bleeding, or bleeding between periods is worth discussing with a clinician.

chunks.title: How long a period lasts
chunks.body: A period commonly lasts about 3 to 7 days, with flow usually heaviest in the first couple of days. Logging your flow helps the app learn your own pattern.

chunks.title: When to see a clinician about your cycle
chunks.body: Consider seeing a clinician for periods that stop unexpectedly, become very heavy or painful, last longer than about a week, or if you're concerned about fertility. This app can't diagnose conditions.

chunks.title: How much water to drink
chunks.body: A common general guideline is roughly 2 to 3 litres of fluids a day for adults, but needs vary with body size, activity, climate and health. Thirst and pale-yellow urine are useful everyday cues.

chunks.title: Signs of dehydration
chunks.body: Dark urine, thirst, dry mouth, headache and tiredness can be signs you need more fluids. Sip water through the day rather than a lot at once.

chunks.title: Do coffee and tea count?
chunks.body: Moderate coffee and tea do contribute to your daily fluids for most people, though very high caffeine can be mildly dehydrating. Water is still the simplest choice.

chunks.title: Urine colour as a hydration cue
chunks.body: Pale straw-coloured urine usually suggests good hydration; dark yellow often means it's time for more fluids. Some vitamins and foods can change the colour.

chunks.title: Hydration around exercise
chunks.body: Drink some water before, during and after activity, especially in heat. For long or intense sessions, replacing electrolytes can help.

chunks.title: Drinking water before bed
chunks.body: Staying hydrated is good, but large amounts right before bed can interrupt sleep with bathroom trips. Spreading fluids through the day helps.

chunks.title: How much sleep adults need
chunks.body: Most adults do best with about 7 to 9 hours of sleep per night. Consistency matters as much as the total — going to bed and waking at similar times helps.

chunks.title: Sleep hygiene basics
chunks.body: A cool, dark, quiet room, a regular schedule, and a wind-down routine support better sleep. Reserve the bed mainly for sleep.

chunks.title: Screens and blue light
chunks.body: Bright screens in the hour before bed can make it harder to fall asleep. Dimming lights and putting devices away earlier may help you wind down.

chunks.title: Caffeine and sleep
chunks.body: Caffeine can stay in your system for many hours, so afternoon and evening coffee can disrupt sleep for some people. Try an earlier cut-off if you sleep poorly.

chunks.title: Why a consistent schedule helps
chunks.body: Waking and sleeping at similar times strengthens your body clock, which can improve how quickly you fall asleep and how rested you feel.

chunks.title: Napping
chunks.body: Short naps of about 10 to 20 minutes earlier in the day can be refreshing. Long or late naps can make it harder to sleep at night.

chunks.title: Sleep debt
chunks.body: Regularly sleeping less than you need builds 'sleep debt', which can affect mood, focus and energy. A few consistent, slightly earlier nights help you recover.

chunks.title: A wind-down routine
chunks.body: A calming routine — dim lights, a warm shower, reading, or gentle stretching — signals your body it's time to sleep. Try to start it around the same time each night.

chunks.title: A reasonable daily step goal
chunks.body: Many people aim for around 8,000 to 10,000 steps a day, but any increase over your current average is beneficial. The app can suggest a goal based on your own recent activity.

chunks.title: Benefits of walking
chunks.body: Regular walking supports heart health, mood, sleep and energy. Even short walks add up over the day.

chunks.title: Breaking up sitting
chunks.body: Standing up and moving for a couple of minutes every half hour or so can offset long periods of sitting. A short walk after meals is an easy habit.

chunks.title: Increasing activity gradually
chunks.body: If you're starting out, build up steps gradually — adding a little each week is more sustainable and gentler on joints than a sudden jump.

chunks.title: Steps vs. active minutes
chunks.body: Steps are a simple daily measure; general guidance also suggests about 150 minutes of moderate activity per week. Brisk walking counts toward both.

chunks.title: Steps and calories
chunks.body: Calories burned from steps depend on your weight, pace and stride, so app estimates are approximate. Consistency matters more than the exact number.

chunks.title: Taking medicine as prescribed
chunks.body: Take medicines at the dose and times your clinician or the label directs. If something is unclear, ask your pharmacist — this app can't give dosing advice.

chunks.title: Remembering your doses
chunks.body: Pairing a dose with a daily routine (like brushing your teeth or a meal) and using reminders makes it easier to stay consistent.

chunks.title: A missed dose (general)
chunks.body: What to do about a missed dose depends on the medicine — some can be taken when you remember, others should be skipped. Check the label or ask your pharmacist; don't double up unless told to.

chunks.title: With or without food
chunks.body: Some medicines work best with food and others on an empty stomach. Follow the label's instruction, and ask your pharmacist if it isn't stated.

chunks.title: Storing medicines
chunks.body: Most medicines keep best in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight and out of reach of children. Some need refrigeration — check the label.

chunks.title: Stopping a medicine
chunks.body: Don't stop a prescribed medicine on your own, even if you feel better — talk to your clinician first, as some need to be tapered.

chunks.title: Blood pressure ranges (general)
chunks.body: As a general guide, a reading around 120/80 mmHg is often considered normal; consistently higher readings are worth discussing with a clinician. A single reading isn't a diagnosis.

chunks.title: Measuring blood pressure at home
chunks.body: Sit quietly for a few minutes, keep your arm supported at heart height, and avoid caffeine or exercise just before. Taking readings at similar times helps you compare.

chunks.title: What can raise blood pressure
chunks.body: Stress, caffeine, salt, poor sleep and recent activity can temporarily raise a reading. Trends over time are more meaningful than any single number.

chunks.title: Blood sugar ranges (general)
chunks.body: General reference points are often around 70–99 mg/dL fasting and under about 140 mg/dL two hours after a meal, but targets are individual. Discuss your own targets with a clinician.

chunks.title: What affects blood sugar
chunks.body: Meals (especially carbohydrates), activity, stress, illness and some medicines all influence blood sugar. Logging context with readings helps you spot patterns.

chunks.title: When to seek care for vitals
chunks.body: Very high or very low readings, or symptoms like chest pain, severe dizziness or confusion, need prompt medical attention. This app is informational and can't diagnose.

chunks.title: Your data stays on your device
chunks.body: DailyMinder's assistant answers from your own logs and a built-in wellness knowledge base entirely on your device. It doesn't send your questions or health data to any server.

chunks.title: Informational, not a diagnosis
chunks.body: The assistant shares general wellness information and patterns from your own data. It is not a medical diagnosis or treatment — always confirm with a qualified clinician or pharmacist.

chunks.title: Spotting between periods
chunks.body: Light spotting between periods can happen around ovulation or with hormonal changes and is often harmless. Frequent, heavy, or unexplained bleeding between periods is worth discussing with a clinician.

chunks.title: Easing period cramps
chunks.body: Gentle movement, a warm compress, staying hydrated, and rest can ease mild period cramps for many people. If pain is severe or stops you doing daily activities, talk to a clinician.

chunks.title: Why track your cycle
chunks.body: Logging your period start, flow, and symptoms helps the app learn your rhythm and gives you a clearer picture of what's typical for you over time.

chunks.title: Everyday vaginal discharge
chunks.body: Clear or white discharge that changes across the cycle is a normal part of a healthy cycle. A sudden change in colour, smell, or itching is worth checking with a clinician.

chunks.title: Alcohol and sleep
chunks.body: A drink may feel relaxing but alcohol tends to fragment sleep later in the night, so you wake less rested. Leaving a few hours between a drink and bedtime helps.

chunks.title: Exercise and sleep
chunks.body: Regular daytime activity generally helps you fall asleep faster and sleep more deeply. Very intense exercise right before bed can be stimulating for some people.

chunks.title: If you can't fall asleep
chunks.body: If you're still awake after about 20 minutes, it can help to get up, do something calm and dim-lit, and return to bed when sleepy — rather than lying there frustrated.

chunks.title: Water first thing
chunks.body: A glass of water in the morning is an easy way to start the day hydrated after a night's sleep. It's a helpful habit, not a strict rule.

chunks.title: Can you drink too much?
chunks.body: Drinking far more water than you need over a short time can dilute your body's salts and is occasionally harmful. For most people, drinking to thirst across the day is a safe guide.

chunks.title: Rest and recovery
chunks.body: Rest days are part of a healthy routine — they let muscles recover and reduce injury risk. Gentle movement like walking or stretching on rest days is fine.

chunks.title: Adding strength work
chunks.body: General guidance suggests muscle-strengthening activity on about two days a week alongside walking. Bodyweight moves like squats or wall push-ups count.

chunks.title: Warming up
chunks.body: A few minutes of easy movement before more vigorous activity warms your muscles and can lower injury risk. Cooling down gently afterward helps too.

chunks.title: Alcohol with medicines
chunks.body: Some medicines interact with alcohol, which can reduce how well they work or increase side effects. Check the label or ask your pharmacist before mixing the two.

chunks.title: Medicine interactions (general)
chunks.body: Different medicines — and some supplements — can affect each other. Keep an up-to-date list of everything you take and share it with your pharmacist or clinician.

chunks.title: Grapefruit and some medicines
chunks.body: Grapefruit can change how the body handles certain medicines. If your label or pharmacist mentions it, it's best to avoid grapefruit and its juice while taking that medicine.

chunks.title: Medicines while travelling
chunks.body: When travelling, keep medicines in your carry-on, bring enough for the trip plus a few spare days, and keep them in their labelled packaging.

chunks.title: Resting heart rate (general)
chunks.body: A typical resting heart rate for adults is often around 60–100 beats per minute, and fitter people can be lower. What matters most is your own usual range over time.

chunks.title: Rechecking a high reading
chunks.body: A single high blood-pressure reading isn't a diagnosis. Rest quietly for a few minutes and recheck; if readings stay high across several days, discuss them with a clinician.

chunks.title: Feeling shaky or lightheaded
chunks.body: Shakiness, sweating, or lightheadedness can sometimes relate to low blood sugar, especially if you take glucose-lowering medicine. Follow your clinician's plan, and seek help for severe or repeated episodes.

chunks.title: A balanced plate
chunks.body: A simple guide is to fill about half your plate with vegetables and fruit, a quarter with whole grains, and a quarter with protein. Variety across the week matters more than any single meal.

chunks.title: Fibre
chunks.body: Fibre from vegetables, fruit, beans and whole grains supports digestion and helps you feel full. Increasing it gradually with plenty of water is easiest on the gut.

chunks.title: Added sugar
chunks.body: Cutting back on sugary drinks and snacks is one of the simplest ways to reduce added sugar. Whole fruit, which also brings fibre and water, is a better everyday choice.

chunks.title: Salt
chunks.body: Most people get more salt than they need, largely from packaged and restaurant food. Cooking at home and tasting before adding more are easy ways to cut back.

chunks.title: Protein at meals
chunks.body: Including a source of protein — beans, eggs, dairy, fish, poultry or tofu — at each meal helps with fullness and maintaining muscle. Spreading it across the day is better than one large serving.

chunks.title: Everyday stress
chunks.body: Regular sleep, movement, time outdoors, and staying connected with people all help buffer everyday stress. If stress feels constant or overwhelming, talking to a professional can help.

chunks.title: A simple breathing reset
chunks.body: Slow breathing — for example in for four counts, out for six — for a minute or two can calm the body's stress response. It's a handy tool before a stressful moment.

chunks.title: Movement and mood
chunks.body: Even a short walk can lift mood and ease tension for many people. Regular activity is one of the most reliable everyday supports for mental wellbeing.

chunks.title: Taking screen breaks
chunks.body: Short breaks from screens — a brief walk, looking into the distance, or stretching — can ease eye strain and help focus. A common reminder is to look away every 20 minutes or so.
